RNASeq: Need for reanalysis?

Rohit Satyam, Alberto Maillo, David Gomez-Cabrero, Arnab Pain

King Abdullah University of Science & Technology, Saudi Arabia

21 October, 2026

Source: vignettes/Need_for_reanalysis.Rmd
Need_for_reanalysis.Rmd

Abstract

This section examines how annotations evolve across successive VEuPathDB releases. As exon–intron boundaries are continually refined with incoming sequencing data, tracking shifts in effective gene length enables users to decide whether existing published datasets warrant reanalysis based on the magnitude of those changes.

Introduction

In the bioinformatics community, it is common to reuse published RNA-seq count or normalized count data without reprocessing, often overlooking important technical differences such as the version of genome annotation. Assembly updates typically include revisions to:

  • GFF files, where gene models and exon‐intron structures are updated, UTRs redefined etc.
  • GAF files, where GO terms are revised based on newly published evidence

For RNA-seq, these updates can substantially affect downstream analyses (e.g., over-representation or pathway enrichment). These changes are often documented in the NEWS sections of VEuPathDB.

For instance, in Plasmodium and Toxoplasma, two key assembly updates were:

  • Release 51 (16 Mar 2021) for PlasmoDB
  • Release 66 (28 Nov 2023) for ToxoDB, which included extensive gene‐model revisions

For RNA-seq, we focus on two annotation features that can affect quantification and downstream biological interpretation. These include changes in:

  1. Number of Genes
  2. Exon–intron boundaries: Measured here using the union of annotated exons per gene. This is an exon-union length, not an RNA-seq fragment-adjusted effective transcript length.

In the example below, we will use Plasmodium and Toxoplasma releases and the plasmoRUtils function getEffLen() to track how effective gene lengths shift across versions.

With release 71 of VEuPathDB, only users with subscription and API key can access the database programmatically. Use usethis::edit_r_environ(scope = "user") to add VEuPathDB API using VEUPATHDB_API_KEY variable. By default, all the functions look for VEUPATHDB_API_KEY variable for API key. Should you store your key using any other variable, supply it using api_key argument in VEuPathDB associated functions.

Assessing Changes in Gene Number

We will compare seven releases (24, 30, 40, 50, 60, 68, and 71) for both Plasmodium and Toxoplasma. From the NEWS section, we know that in Plasmodium, several loci initially annotated as rRNAs, lncRNAs, or coding genes were later removed, and the mitochondrial genome of PF3D7 was revised in 2019. Similarly, Toxoplasma TGME49 gene models underwent extensive updates in release 66.

library(plasmoRUtils)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggpubr) 

releases <- c(24, 30, 40, 50, 60, 68, 71) 

getEffLenVEuPath <- function(
    url,
    api_key = Sys.getenv("VEUPATHDB_API_KEY"),
    timeout = 120
) {

  if (!nzchar(api_key)) {
    stop(
      "VEuPathDB API key is missing.",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".gff")
  on.exit(unlink(tmp), add = TRUE)

  httr2::request(url) |>
    httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(api_key) |>
    httr2::req_timeout(timeout) |>
    httr2::req_perform(path = tmp)

  getEffLen(tmp)
}


## Fetching GFFs from PlasmoDB and calculating effective lengths
pf3d7.gffs <- lapply(releases, function(x){
 paste0("https://plasmodb.org/a/service/raw-files/release-",x,"/Pfalciparum3D7/gff/data/PlasmoDB-",x,"_Pfalciparum3D7.gff") %>% getEffLenVEuPath() 
}) %>% setNames(releases) 

## Fetching GFFs from ToxoDB and calculating effective lengths
tgme49.gffs <- lapply(releases, function(x){
  Sys.sleep(20) ## because VEuPathDB gives timeout if too many files are fetched
  paste0("https://toxodb.org/a/service/raw-files/release-",x,"/TgondiiME49/gff/data/ToxoDB-",x,"_TgondiiME49.gff") %>% getEffLenVEuPath()
}) %>% setNames(releases)

## Let's plot changes in number of genes 
pf3d7.ngenes<- lapply(pf3d7.gffs, nrow)  %>% setNames(releases) %>% plyr::ldply()
tgme49.ngenes<- lapply(tgme49.gffs, nrow)  %>% setNames(releases) %>% plyr::ldply()

ggpubr::ggline(pf3d7.ngenes,x=".id",y="V1", label = TRUE, color = "#2595be", fill = "#2595be")+labs(x="Releases",y="No. of Genes")+theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))


ggpubr::ggline(tgme49.ngenes,x=".id",y="V1", label = TRUE, color = "#2595be", fill = "#2595be")+labs(x="Releases",y="No. of Genes")+theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))

The plotted values describe the number of annotated gene IDs with computable exon-union lengths in each selected release. These counts should not be interpreted as a direct count of genes gained or lost without matching gene identifiers across releases.

Assessing the difference in Effective gene lengths

To compare relative variation in exon-union length across releases, we calculate the coefficient of variation:

CV (%) = 100 × standard deviation / mean

A gene with unchanged exon-union length across releases has CV = 0. Higher CV indicates greater relative variability; for example, a 100-bp difference matters more for a 200-bp feature than for a 5,000-bp feature.

We will calculate CV using following steps:

  1. Because gene IDs may vary across releases, we will first convert unambiguous legacy gene IDs to current IDs using toGeneid() and retain genes represented in all selected releases.
  2. In old annotations like release 24, some genes coding for multiple transcripts are present as separate gene entries each coding for 1 transcripts often denoted by versions before them such as PF3D7_0618900.1,PF3D7_0618900.2. This issue has been fixed in latest releases. To handle this we will remove the versions from gene IDs and average the exon-union lengths for duplicate legacy gene rows for descriptive comparison; this does not replace transcript-aware quantification.
  3. Calculate CV for genes with complete release coverage and identify those with CV greater than zero.
# map only unambiguous legacy IDs to a current gene ID.
map_legacy_ids <- function(df, annotation, organism, database) {
  legacy <- setdiff(unique(df$GeneID), unique(annotation$`Gene ID`))
  if (!length(legacy)) return(df)
  map <- toGeneid(legacy, from = "old", to = "ensembl") %>%
    dplyr::select(`Input ID`, `Gene ID`) %>%
    dplyr::distinct() %>%
    dplyr::group_by(`Input ID`) %>%
    dplyr::filter(dplyr::n_distinct(`Gene ID`) == 1L) %>%
    dplyr::ungroup()
  ix <- match(df$GeneID, map$`Input ID`)
  replace <- !is.na(ix)
  df$GeneID[replace] <- map$`Gene ID`[ix[replace]]
  df
}


###  Step1
# Remove version suffix from GeneIDs
df <- pf3d7.gffs %>% plyr::ldply() %>%
  mutate(GeneID = sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", GeneID)) 

annot <- getTable(org = "Plasmodium falciparum 3D7", db = "plasmodb")
df <- map_legacy_ids(df, annot, "Plasmodium falciparum 3D7", "plasmodb") 
subdf <- df %>% dplyr::filter(GeneID %in% annot$`Gene ID`) 

###  Step 2 
# Aggregate length per gene across releases
df_agg <- subdf %>%
  group_by(.id, GeneID) %>%
  summarise(mean_length = round(mean(Length, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = GeneID, values_from = mean_length, values_fill = NA) %>%
  column_to_rownames(".id") %>%
  as.matrix() %>% { stopifnot(setequal(rownames(.), as.character(releases))); .[, colSums(!is.na(.)) == length(releases), drop = FALSE] } 

###  Step 3
# Coefficient of variation across releases
cv <- apply(df_agg, 2, function(x) (sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) * 100) %>%
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)

## How many genes have their effective exon length change >100 bp between versions 50 and 71
table((df_agg["71", ] - df_agg["50", ]) > 100) ##4434
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>  1198  4434

## Check for how many genes the effective length has changed
table(cv > 0, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>  1095  4537
hist(cv[is.finite(cv)], main = "Variation in exon-union length", xlab = "CV (%)") 


## Let's filter top 20 genes whose effective length has changed drastically and see what they are

annot %>%
  dplyr::select(`Gene ID`, `Product Description`) %>% 
  dplyr::distinct(`Gene ID`, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(`Gene ID` %in% utils::head(names(cv), 20L)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(cv = unname(cv[match(`Gene ID`, names(cv))])) %>% 
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(cv))

# plot top 2 variable genes
plts <- names(cv)[1:2] %>%
  lapply(function(gid) {
    df %>%
      filter(GeneID == gid) %>%
      ggpubr::ggline(x = ".id", y = "Length",color = "#2595be", fill = "#2595be") +
      labs(title = gid, x = "Release", y = "Effective Length") +
      theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))
  })

library(sjPlot)
plot_grid(plts)

These comparisons show how annotation changes can alter exon-union lengths. An observed difference in gene models motivates reassessing older quantifications, but does not itself prove that every corresponding RNA-seq read count will change.

If you are working on annotation of hypothetical genes, you should be cautious about which assembly you use since your gene might appear to be down regulated as per old annotation but this might change with change in the current annotation.

Let’s recycle the code above for Toxoplasma.

###  Step1
# Remove version suffix from GeneIDs
df <- tgme49.gffs %>% plyr::ldply() %>%
  mutate(GeneID = sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", GeneID)) # strip terminal version suffix

annot <- getTable(org = "Toxoplasma gondii ME49", db = "toxodb")
df <- map_legacy_ids(df, annot, "Toxoplasma gondii ME49", "toxodb")
subdf <- df %>% dplyr::filter(GeneID %in% annot$`Gene ID`)

###  Step 2 
# Aggregate length per gene across releases
df_agg <- subdf %>%
  group_by(.id, GeneID) %>%
  summarise(mean_length = round(mean(Length, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = GeneID, values_from = mean_length, values_fill = NA) %>%
  column_to_rownames(".id") %>%
  as.matrix() %>% { stopifnot(setequal(rownames(.), as.character(releases))); .[, colSums(!is.na(.)) == length(releases), drop = FALSE] } 

###  Step 3
# Coefficient of variation across releases
cv <- apply(df_agg, 2, function(x) (sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) * 100) %>%
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)

## How many genes have their effective exon length change >100 bp
table((df_agg["71", ] - df_agg["60", ]) > 100) # 2136

table(cv > 0, useNA = "ifany")

The same procedure shows which shared Toxoplasma genes changed their exon-union lengths between the selected releases.

Discussion

The scope of reannotation influences the comparability of legacy datasets; whether reprocessing is required depends on the type of analysis, genome assembly, annotation changes and quantification method. A prior survey of PlasmoDB datasets suggested that many published analyses relied on annotations predating release 51; any reported counts should be interpreted relative to the survey date rather than as live database statistics. For analyses sensitive to gene-model changes, reprocessing against a documented, up-to-date reference is preferable when compatible raw data are available. When reanalysis is warranted, users should document the precise reference assembly, annotation release and quantification workflow.
